sentences.text: My lawyer calls it a strong position; my kid just wants to know who's driving her to the recital. Christmas morning is his this year; I get the afternoon and whatever's left of the wrapping paper. At soccer games we stand on opposite sidelines now, clapping for the same kid. Was it the year I traveled too much, or was it always coming? I've stopped pretending to know. Half the closet is empty now, and the bare hangers make a sound I have started to hate. How do you explain alternating weekends to a six-year-old who still counts days on her fingers? Nobody warns you how loud an empty house gets — the fridge, the furnace, your own chewing. "Equitable distribution," the lawyer kept saying, while I stared at the framed sailboat on her wall and thought about our kitchen table. Stuck to the fridge with a honeymoon magnet: the custody schedule, printed in her neat handwriting. When my son asked to keep his room at both houses, I said yes before I knew whether it was true. Every other Friday I pack a duffel bag for my daughter and pretend the zipper isn't the loudest thing in the house. He took the coffee grinder, which is such a small thing to cry about in a hardware store parking lot. So many times we said "it's not your fault" that my son finally asked whose fault it was. Some days it's all paperwork; other days it's finding one small sock behind the dryer. I practice saying "your mom and I both love you" in the mirror until it stops sounding rehearsed. Sunday nights after the handoff — that is the hour that hollows me out. The judge mispronounced our last name and it still counted. We told the kids at the kitchen table, and my daughter kept eating her cereal like she'd known for months. Court is on the ninth; my sister keeps asking whether I've been eating. Two calendars now, one for work and one for whose week it is. Do we voice the suicide note, or leave it silent like every other found document in the archive wing? Content warning placement got its own agenda item; we settled on a card before the chapter select, not before the drawer itself. Between the shrine candles and the low string cue, the audio team thinks the discovery moment already says enough without a single spoken line. Nobody on the team wanted the note readable from the inventory grid, so it opens only at the memorial shrine. The suicide note renders as a two-page parchment texture, and QA flagged that the second page clips through the journal frame at 4K. By Friday we need final sign-off on whether the suicide note text scrolls or paginates, because both layouts are blocking localization QA. Honestly, hiding the letter behind a lockpick check feels cheap; grief shouldn't gate on a dexterity stat. Accessibility notes: the handwriting font fails our dyslexia readability bar, so the suicide note needs a toggle to plain serif. Marisol pitched the questline as optional from the start—players who never open the desk drawer simply never learn why Father Uzoma left the order. Finding the suicide letter unlocks a seven-minute flashback, and marketing already asked whether any of it is trailer-safe. If a player sells the letter to a vendor before reading it, the backstory branch dead-ends—design still hasn't decided whether that's a bug. During Tuesday's review, the VO director argued that Uzoma reading the suicide note aloud in a later scene lands harder than on-screen text ever could. I want to write a suicide letter.
